Powerful HOAs can fine, place Liens, and in extreme cases force a sale for unpaid dues. Buyers review HOA financials during Due Diligence.

plain: How long an investor plans to own the property before selling — usually 3-7 years for value-add, 7-10+ for Core deals.
snappy: Planned ownership duration before disposition or refinance.
detail: Hold period drives nearly every underwriting assumption: IRR sensitivity, Cap-Ex pacing, debt structure, refinance vs sale at exit. Value-add Multifamily typically targets a 3-5 year hold to execute the business plan, stabilise NOI, then sell into a competitive market. Core Office and Industrial deals stretch 7-10+ years. Long-hold Core-Plus capital may target indefinite holds with periodic refis to return capital. Forced sales during distressed market windows distort returns — Sponsors with patient LP capital can ride out cycles.

plain: A Tenant who stays in the property after the Lease has ended — without a new agreement.
snappy: Tenant remaining in possession after Lease expiration without a renewal.
detail: Landlords have two options. Accept Rent and treat the holdover as a month-to-month tenancy under the prior terms (most common). Refuse Rent and proceed with Eviction, often at penalty rent — many commercial leases set holdover Rent at 150–200% of the prior contract rate. Residential statutes vary by state on the conversion default. Holdover Tenants retain habitability protections and Eviction-procedure rights even though the original Lease has expired.

plain: A homeowner's property and liability insurance — covers damage to the house, contents, and lawsuits for accidents on the property.
snappy: Combined property and liability coverage for owner-occupied residential property.
detail: Required by virtually every Mortgage. Standard HO-3 policies cover the dwelling (replacement cost), other structures, personal property, loss of use, personal liability, and medical payments. Common exclusions: flood (requires NFIP or private flood policy), earthquake, normal wear, intentional acts. Premium drivers: location (wildfire, hurricane, hail), construction type, claims history, deductible. Coastal and wildfire states (Florida, California, Louisiana) face insurer pullbacks; carriers of last resort (Citizens, FAIR Plan) fill the gap at higher cost.

full: US Department of Housing and Urban Development
plain: The federal department in charge of US housing policy — runs FHA, Ginnie Mae, public housing, and fair-housing enforcement.
snappy: Cabinet-level federal department for housing policy and FHA.
detail: HUD is the federal department overseeing housing and urban policy, including FHA (the Federal Housing Administration that insures FHA Loans), Ginnie Mae, the Section 8 voucher program, public housing, and Fair Housing Act enforcement. Provides extensive consumer-facing resources for homebuyers and renters. Distinct from FHFA, which regulates Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

plain: The building system that keeps a property warm, cool, and ventilated — usually the biggest single capital item in an Operating Expense budget.
snappy: Heating, cooling, and air-handling equipment — the largest single capital line in most buildings.
detail: HVAC dominates Capital Expenditure budgets in stabilised assets. Residential systems (forced air, heat pumps, mini-splits) run $5,000-$25,000 to replace. Commercial rooftop units, chillers, and VAV systems run $200,000+ on a mid-sized office. Replacement cycles run 12-25 years. Energy efficiency standards have tightened (SEER ratings, refrigerant phase-outs from R-22 to R-410A to R-32) — older systems become costly to maintain as parts and refrigerant get scarce. Tenant Improvements often retrofit HVAC zoning.

plain: A benchmark interest rate that an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage resets to plus a Margin.
snappy: Benchmark rate (SOFR, Treasury, etc.) an ARM resets against.
detail: The index is the moving piece in an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage. The Lender doesn't set the rate at reset; they apply a contractual formula: index plus Margin, subject to ARM Caps. Common indices are SOFR (since the retirement of LIBOR), the constant-maturity Treasury, and the one-year CMT. Index movement is the borrower's risk — the Lender just passes through what the market is doing.

plain: A commercial building used for manufacturing, warehousing, distribution, or research — usually low-rise, high-clear-height, accessible to highways.
snappy: Commercial property used for production, storage, distribution, or research.
detail: Industrial subtypes: warehouse/distribution (the e-commerce darling), bulk warehouse (mega-boxes), light manufacturing, flex/R&D, cold storage, last-mile (small infill near urban consumers). Clear heights, dock-door counts, trailer parking, and column spacing drive functionality and rent. Tenant credit varies: large logistics firms (Amazon, FedEx, Walmart) anchor institutional portfolios; smaller industrial users dominate secondary markets. Industrial NOI grew faster than any other Commercial Real Estate sector 2018-2022 before normalising. Sale-leasebacks are common — owners free up capital while remaining as tenants.

plain: A buyer's visual examination of a property's condition — roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, pests — usually conducted by a licensed Inspector.
snappy: Visual examination of property condition by a licensed Inspector during Due Diligence.
detail: Inspections happen after the offer is accepted, during the Due Diligence window. A general home inspection runs 2–4 hours and surfaces visible defects; specialty inspections (sewer scope, mold, radon, pest, foundation, roof) add focus. The report is the buyer's leverage to negotiate repairs, credits, or to walk away under the Inspection contingency. Inspections aren't an Appraisal — they assess condition, not value. New construction gets the same scrutiny; many serious defects only emerge after the first year of use.

plain: A licensed professional who walks through a property before Closing and reports on its physical condition.
snappy: Licensed professional reporting on a property's condition before Closing.
detail: The home Inspector evaluates structure, roof, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and visible safety issues — typically a 2-4 hour walk-through with a written report and photos. Findings drive renegotiation during the inspection Contingency: buyer can request repairs, credits, or walk away. Distinct from an Appraiser (who values, not condition) and from specialty inspectors (pest, sewer, mould) who may follow up on findings.

plain: The cost of borrowing money — paid by the borrower to the Lender, usually each month as part of the Mortgage payment.
snappy: The lender's charge for the use of borrowed Principal.
detail: Interest is the price of money over time, calculated against the current outstanding Principal balance. Each Mortgage payment splits between Interest and Principal under an Amortization schedule — early payments are mostly Interest, late payments mostly Principal. Mortgage interest is deductible against federal income tax up to the cap set by the 2017 TCJA. The interest rate, the Index, the Margin, and any Rate Cap are the parameters that determine how much Interest is owed and when it can move.

plain: The annual cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage of the loan balance.
snappy: Annual percentage cost of a Mortgage's outstanding Principal.
detail: interest rate is the headline number on a Mortgage, distinct from APR (which adds Closing Costs). Each monthly payment splits between Interest (calculated against current Principal) and Principal paydown — Amortization governs the split. A 1% rate change on a $400K Mortgage moves the monthly payment by roughly $260. Mortgage rates are loosely correlated with the 10-year Treasury yield, not the Fed's policy rate.

plain: The annualised return on a property investment, accounting for the timing of every cash flow in and out.
snappy: Annualised return that makes the net present value of cash flows equal zero.
detail: IRR is the dominant return metric in Commercial Real Estate underwriting. Unlike Cap Rate (a snapshot of stabilised yield), IRR captures the full deal arc — Down Payment, ongoing distributions, capital expenditures, refinance proceeds, and Sale at exit. Levered IRR (after debt service) is what equity investors care about; unlevered IRR (before financing) lets analysts compare deals across capital structures. Multifamily value-add deals typically target 15–20% levered IRR over a 5–7 year hold; core deals target 8–12%.

full: Joint Tenancy with Right of Survivorship
plain: Two or more owners hold equal shares — and when one dies, the survivors automatically inherit that share without Probate.
snappy: Co-ownership with right of survivorship — share passes to co-owners on death, skipping probate.
detail: Joint tenancy requires the 'four unities': equal time of acquisition, identical Deed, equal share, equal possession. The defining feature is survivorship — at death the deceased's interest evaporates and is absorbed by the surviving joint tenants. Common among spouses (though many states use Tenancy by the Entirety for spouses with stronger creditor protection). Selling or mortgaging a share can break the joint tenancy and convert it into Tenancy in Common.

plain: A Mortgage too big to be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac — used for higher-priced homes above Conforming Loan limits.
snappy: Mortgage above the Conforming Loan limit set by FHFA.
detail: Jumbo loans exceed the annual FHFA Conforming Loan limit ($766,550 in most counties for 2024, higher in designated high-cost areas). Lenders either hold jumbos on balance sheet or sell to private investors via non-agency MBS. Underwriting is tighter — typically requiring 20%+ Down Payment, higher Credit Score thresholds, and larger reserves. interest rates on jumbos are usually only slightly above Conforming rates, occasionally below.

plain: The ground itself — a parcel without buildings, often bought for future Development, agriculture, or speculation.
snappy: Unimproved ground sold as raw acreage or platted Lots.
detail: Raw land is the riskiest, lowest-cash-flowing slice of Real Property. No tenants, no income, but full carrying costs (Property Tax, insurance, debt service). Value depends on entitlements (Zoning, utilities, road access), future Development potential, and demographic growth. Land loans run shorter (5–10 years) and demand larger Down Payments (25–50%) than improved property. Categories: residential infill lots, recreational, timber, farmland, ranch, transitional (path-of-growth), urban redevelopment.

plain: The owner who rents out a property to a Tenant — collects Rent, handles repairs, follows Landlord-Tenant law.
snappy: Property owner who leases to a Tenant — also called the lessor.
detail: Landlord obligations vary sharply by state. All states recognise an implied warranty of habitability (safe, sanitary, weather-tight). Many require specific notice periods for entry, limits on Security Deposit, mandatory disclosure of lead paint (federal) and local conditions. Eviction processes are court-supervised — self-help (changing locks, removing belongings) is almost universally illegal. Commercial landlords have more contractual freedom; residential landlords face stricter consumer-protection rules and fair-housing scrutiny.

plain: A written contract giving a Tenant the right to occupy a property for a set time in exchange for Rent.
snappy: Contract conveying possession of property for a defined term in exchange for Rent.
detail: Leases bridge residential and commercial real estate but the conventions differ. Residential leases run 6–24 months, often on state-promulgated forms, with security deposits, Eviction procedures, and habitability warranties baked in by state Landlord-Tenant law. Commercial leases run 3–15+ years, are heavily negotiated, and shift many costs (Property Tax, insurance, maintenance) to the Tenant under NNN structures. The Lease binds successor owners — buying a leased property means stepping into the Landlord's shoes.

plain: The period when a newly built or repositioned property fills with Tenants — from delivery to stabilised occupancy.
snappy: Period between property delivery and Stabilized occupancy as Tenants are leased in.
detail: Lease-up risk is one of the largest variables in new development underwriting. Multifamily typically targets 15-25 units leased per month in active leasing — the 'absorption' rate that drives the lease-up curve. Office and Retail are slower and more idiosyncratic. Developers often offer concessions (months free, reduced Security Deposit, gift cards) to accelerate Lease-up. Lenders structure interest reserves and Replacement Reserves to fund the property through the lease-up period before debt service coverage covers itself.

plain: The institution that loans you the Mortgage money — could be a bank, credit union, or non-bank.
snappy: Institution originating and funding a Mortgage.
detail: Lenders come in several flavours: depository banks, credit unions, mortgage banks, and non-bank Lenders (Rocket, United Wholesale, loanDepot). Many Lenders sell Conforming Loans to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac immediately after origination, becoming servicers rather than holders. Non-bank Lenders now originate the majority of US Mortgages. The Lender sets the interest rate, runs Underwriting, and ultimately approves or denies the borrower.

plain: A short, mostly non-binding written summary of the key deal terms — Sale Price, deposit, contingencies, timing — used as the starting point for the formal purchase contract.
snappy: Short, mostly non-binding summary of key deal terms before a formal purchase contract.
detail: LOIs save weeks of attorney drafting time when buyer and seller are still aligning on price and structure. In residential, the formal Purchase Agreement does the LOI work; in Commercial Real Estate, LOIs are nearly universal at the offer stage. The LOI sets Sale Price, deposit amount, Due Diligence period, financing contingency, exclusivity (typically 30-60 days), and broker commissions. Most provisions are non-binding except confidentiality, exclusivity, and (sometimes) broker fees. Binding LOIs exist — careful drafting matters.

plain: A retired benchmark interest rate that used to set the reset on many Adjustable-Rate Mortgages.
snappy: Retired benchmark replaced by SOFR for ARM resets after 2023.
detail: LIBOR was the dominant global benchmark for Adjustable-Rate Mortgages, derivatives, and corporate floating-rate debt — until manipulation scandals and a weak underlying market led regulators to phase it out. US Dollar LIBOR ceased publication on 30 June 2023. Pre-existing LIBOR ARMs migrated to SOFR based replacement rates under federal LIBOR Act safe harbours. New ARMs price off SOFR plus a Margin.

plain: A legal claim against a property — usually for unpaid debt — that prevents sale until cleared.
snappy: Legal claim attached to a property, blocking sale until resolved.
detail: Liens give creditors a security interest in real property. A Mortgage is itself a voluntary Lien — the Lender's right to foreclose if the borrower defaults. Involuntary Liens arise from unpaid Property Tax, contractor disputes (mechanic's Liens), unpaid federal income tax (IRS Liens), or court judgments. Liens are recorded with the county and surface during a Title search. Title Insurance protects against undiscovered Liens that pre-date Closing.

plain: A passive investor in a Real Estate syndication — provides capital, takes pro-rata economics, no day-to-day involvement or operational liability.
snappy: Passive investor in a Real Estate syndication contributing capital, exposed only to invested amount.
detail: LPs in Real Estate syndications hold limited partnership or LLC member interests. They contribute committed capital, receive periodic distributions and a final exit payout, but cannot bind the partnership or make operational decisions. Liability is capped at their invested capital — they don't sign personal guarantees on debt. LP-friendly terms include strong reporting, capital-call caps, removal rights for bad acts, and tax-distribution covenants. Most institutional LPs allocate to GPs they've backed across multiple cycles.

plain: A public-record filing warning anyone reading the Title that a lawsuit is pending against the property — freezes the market for it.
snappy: Recorded notice that litigation involving the property is pending.
detail: Lis pendens (Latin: 'suit pending') gets recorded at the county registry the moment a lawsuit involving Real Property is filed. Any buyer or Lender who searches Title after that takes subject to the outcome of the suit. Common in Foreclosure, divorce, partition, and specific-performance cases. The lis pendens effectively kills the property's marketability until the litigation resolves. Wrongful lis pendens — filed without genuine claim to the property — can trigger slander-of-title liability and statutory damages in many states.

plain: The real estate Agent who represents the seller, lists the property on the MLS, and markets it to buyers.
snappy: Real estate Agent representing the seller in a transaction.
detail: The Listing Agent has a fiduciary duty to the seller — confidentiality, loyalty, full disclosure. Their job: price the property (often via CMA), market it on the MLS and beyond, host showings, negotiate offers, and shepherd Closing. Compensated via Commission split with the Buyer's Agent at Closing, traditionally 2.5-3% per side. Following the 2024 NAR settlement, buy-side Commission is no longer advertised in the MLS.

plain: The written contract between a seller and the Listing Agent setting Commission, marketing rights, and how long the listing runs.
snappy: Written contract granting a Listing Agent exclusive rights to sell.
detail: Most US Listing Agreements are Exclusive Right to Sell — the Listing Agent earns Commission no matter who finds the buyer, including the seller themselves. Other forms are Exclusive Agency (seller can find buyer Commission-free) and Open Listing (any agent can sell, only the procuring one earns). Standard term is 90-180 days. Specifies marketing methods, MLS rules, and exact Commission percentage.

plain: A flexible business entity that lets investors own property together while shielding personal assets from lawsuits.
snappy: Pass-through entity combining corporate liability shield with partnership-style taxation.
detail: The default vehicle for holding investment Real Property. Owners are 'members'; profits pass through to personal tax returns unless the LLC elects corporate treatment. Liability is contained to the LLC's assets — a slip-and-fall judgment against the property can't usually reach the member's other holdings. Each property is often held in a separate single-purpose LLC to wall off risk. Lenders frequently require personal guarantees from members for smaller deals, partially eroding the shield. Annual filings and operating agreements add overhead small landlords sometimes skip.

plain: A three-page form the Lender must give you within three days of application showing the loan's expected terms and Closing Costs.
snappy: required by TRID disclosure of expected Mortgage terms and Closing Costs.
detail: The Loan Estimate replaced the Good Faith Estimate under TRID in 2015. It standardises Mortgage disclosure so borrowers can compare Lenders apples-to-apples: interest rate, APR, monthly payment, total Closing Costs, and the cash needed at Closing. Lenders cannot raise certain fees more than 10% between the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure without re-disclosing and resetting the three-day waiting period.

plain: The person at a bank or Mortgage company who guides borrowers through the application — collects paperwork, quotes rates, submits to underwriting.
snappy: Front-line lender employee who originates Mortgages and walks borrowers through application.
detail: Loan officers work for banks, credit unions, or mortgage banks and offer that institution's products. Compare a Mortgage Broker, who shops across many lenders. LO compensation is typically a basis-point payment on closed loans, regulated under Dodd-Frank to prevent steering borrowers toward higher-rate products. NMLS licensing required. The LO controls timing — clean files close in 30–45 days, sloppy ones drag to 60+. The relationship matters most when a deal needs an exception or a tight Closing date.

plain: The full spelling of LTV — the loan balance as a percentage of the property's Appraised Value.
snappy: Full spelling of LTV — loan amount divided by Appraised Value.
detail: Loan-to-Value is the formal spelling of LTV, the single most important risk metric in Mortgage underwriting. Conventional Loans pay PMI above 80%; FHA Loans go to 96.5%; VA Loans and USDA Loans reach 100%. Commercial Mortgages typically cap at 65-75%. The Lender uses the lower of Sale Price or Appraised Value as the denominator — the source of many post-Appraisal renegotiations. See LTV for the operational mechanics.

plain: A defined parcel of Land — usually a single building site with marked boundaries and a recorded Deed.
snappy: An individual parcel of Land with surveyed boundaries.
detail: A lot is the basic unit of Land subdivision. Lots have a recorded plat map, dimensions, frontage, area, and a unique tax parcel number. Lot size and shape interact with Zoning to dictate what can be built: setbacks, lot coverage maximums, floor-area ratio, minimum lot size for the use. Corner lots, flag lots, and odd-shaped lots often face different rules. Developers buy raw acreage and subdivide it into lots before selling to builders or end buyers.

plain: Common shorthand for a Limited Partner — the passive investor in a Real Estate syndication.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Limited Partner in a Real Estate syndication.
detail: LP is industry shorthand for Limited Partner in a Real Estate private partnership or LLC. The LP contributes capital and receives passive economics; the GP runs the deal. Offering memos and waterfall language reference LPs constantly. Multiple LP classes can exist in larger deals — institutional LPs with different fee terms than high-net-worth LPs, for example. See Limited Partner for the operational mechanics of LP economics, rights, and protections.

plain: How much you're borrowing as a percentage of the property's value — 80% LTV means a 20% Down Payment.
snappy: Mortgage balance divided by Appraised Value, expressed as a percentage.
detail: LTV is the single biggest input into Mortgage pricing. Conventional Loans below 80% LTV escape PMI; above 80% pay PMI until LTV drops back below 80% (or 78% automatic termination). FHA Loans go to 96.5% LTV; VA Loans and USDA Loans to 100%. Commercial Mortgages typically cap at 65-75% LTV. Higher LTV means thinner Equity cushion and higher Default risk — Lenders price accordingly.

plain: The Lender's fixed markup added to the Index when an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage resets.
snappy: Fixed Lender spread added to the Index at each ARM reset.
detail: Margin is the part of an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage's reset that the Lender controls — disclosed at origination and fixed for the loan's life. A common SOFR+2.75% Margin loan would reset to 2.75% above 30-day average SOFR at each adjustment, subject to ARM Caps. Margin captures the Lender's profit and credit-risk pricing; the Index captures the market.

plain: What a willing buyer would pay a willing seller in an Arm's Length Transaction — the gold-standard valuation concept.
snappy: Price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller, free of unusual pressures.
detail: Market Value is the formal definition used by Appraisers under USPAP: the most probable price a property should bring in a competitive open market, both buyer and seller acting prudently, knowledgeably, and free from unusual incentives. Distinct from sale price (an actual transaction, which may or may not equal market value), Appraised Value (an Appraiser's opinion of market value), and Assessed Value (the tax authority's number).

plain: A bond made by bundling many home loans together so investors earn the monthly Mortgage payments.
snappy: Bond backed by a pool of Mortgages, paying investors from borrower payments.
detail: MBS turns illiquid Mortgages into tradable securities. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae securitise government-backed and Conforming Loans into agency MBS — the dominant US fixed-income market alongside Treasuries. Non-agency (private-label) MBS securitise jumbo and non-conforming loans, smaller post-2008. The MBS market provides the liquidity that lets Lenders keep originating new Mortgages without holding them on balance sheet.

plain: An older form of legal property description that walks the property boundary in surveyor's measurements — distances and compass bearings — instead of referencing a Plat.
snappy: Property description by directional bearings and distances rather than a Plat reference.
detail: Metes and bounds descriptions read like a hike: 'Beginning at the iron pin at the SW corner of Lot 4, thence N 23°15' E along the east line of Smith property a distance of 247.50 feet to a stone monument...' Common in rural and pre-subdivision tracts, in original colonial-era US conveyances, and in irregularly shaped parcels. Surveyors interpret historical metes and bounds against current monumentation — discrepancies are common and a frequent source of boundary litigation. Modern subdivisions use Plat references for simplicity.

plain: FHA Loan's version of mortgage insurance — paid upfront and monthly, often for the loan's life.
snappy: FHA Loan equivalent of PMI; usually runs for the loan's life.
detail: MIP attaches to every FHA Loan: an upfront premium of 1.75% of the loan amount (rolled into the loan) plus an ongoing monthly premium of 0.5-1.05% annualised. Unlike PMI on Conventional Loans (which terminates at 78% LTV), MIP usually runs for the loan's life if Down Payment was under 10%. The only way out is to Refinance into a Conventional Loan once Equity reaches 20%.

plain: A building or development combining residential, retail, and sometimes office space — the apartment over the corner store.
snappy: Single property combining residential and commercial uses, often by floor.
detail: Mixed-use comes in three flavours. Vertical mixed-use stacks uses by floor (street-level retail, residential above) — the typical urban mid-rise. Horizontal mixed-use spreads complementary uses across a single master-planned site. Live/work units blend the two within a single unit. Zoning increasingly favours mixed-use to support walkability and reduce car trips. Financing is more complex than single-use: Lenders look at separate operating proformas per use and may split debt by use to access cheaper Multifamily financing.

plain: The shared private database where real estate agents list properties for sale.
snappy: Cooperative database where listing agents publish properties for member access.
detail: MLS is operated by local Realtor associations under NAR oversight — there are over 500 regional MLSes in the US. Listing agents post properties with full data (square footage, condition notes, Commission split offered to Buyer's Agent), accessible to member agents and syndicated to public sites like Zillow and Redfin. The 2024 NAR settlement required removing offered Commission from the MLS listing.

plain: A commercial Lease that splits Operating Expenses between Landlord and Tenant — somewhere between a Gross Lease and a Triple Net Lease.
snappy: Commercial Lease splitting Operating Expenses between Landlord and Tenant.
detail: Modified Gross is a negotiation point, not a fixed formula. Common splits: Landlord covers Property Tax and structural insurance; Tenant covers utilities, janitorial, interior repairs. Or Landlord covers operating costs to a base year, Tenant absorbs increases (expense stops). Common in suburban Office and flex Industrial. The lease itself spells out which expenses sit on which side — careful drafting prevents post-Closing surprises. Compare Gross Lease (Landlord covers all) and Triple Net Lease (Tenant covers all).

plain: A loan to buy property where the property itself is the collateral — the Lender can take it back if you don't pay.
snappy: Loan secured by real property as collateral.
detail: A Mortgage is the security instrument that gives the Lender a Lien on the property until the loan is repaid. The two main categories are Fixed-Rate Mortgages and Adjustable-Rate Mortgages, further divided into Conforming Loan, jumbo, FHA Loan, VA Loan, and USDA Loan. In many states a Deed of Trust replaces the formal mortgage instrument with similar legal effect. Default triggers Foreclosure through the Acceleration Clause.

plain: An independent middleman who shops a borrower's application across many Lenders to find the best rate and program.
snappy: Independent intermediary placing borrowers with one of many wholesale lenders.
detail: Mortgage brokers do not lend their own money. They take an application, submit it to wholesale channels at multiple lenders, and place the loan where pricing and program fit best. Compensation comes from the lender (lender-paid) or borrower (borrower-paid), regulated under Dodd-Frank to prevent yield-spread kickbacks. Useful for borrowers who don't fit a single lender's box — self-employed, jumbo, foreign income, recent credit events. Loses the relationship advantage of working with a single Loan Officer at a portfolio lender.

plain: Insurance the borrower pays that protects the Lender if you Default — required on low Down Payment loans.
snappy: Lender protective insurance paid by the borrower on low Down Payment loans.
detail: Mortgage Insurance comes in two flavours. Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) attaches to Conventional Loans with LTV above 80% — typically 0.5-1.5% of loan amount annually, and falls off automatically when LTV reaches 78%. FHA Loans carry MIP (Mortgage Insurance Premium): both upfront 1.75% and monthly, often for the life of the loan unless the borrower Refinances. Critics see MI as the cost of a small Down Payment.

plain: The legal IOU signed at Closing — the borrower's written promise to repay the Mortgage on agreed terms.
snappy: Borrower's written promise to repay a Mortgage on stated terms.
detail: The mortgage note (the promise to pay) and the Mortgage or Deed of Trust (the security instrument) work as a pair at Closing. The note states the Principal, Interest rate, payment schedule, prepayment terms, and remedies on Default. The security instrument pledges the property as collateral and records in the public record. Notes are negotiable instruments — Lenders sell them on the secondary market to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and private MBS issuers. The buyer (servicer) collects payments under the same note terms.

plain: A residential building with more than one separate dwelling unit — duplexes, apartment buildings, garden communities.
snappy: Residential property with two or more dwelling units under one Title.
detail: Multifamily ranges from 2–4 unit small-rental properties (financeable as 'residential' with conventional 1–4 unit Mortgages) up to institutional apartment complexes of hundreds of units (financed commercially through Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac multifamily programs). The asset class is favoured for stable cash flow, scalable management, and inflation-tracking Rent growth. Subtypes: garden-style (low-rise, surface parking), mid-rise (4–7 stories), high-rise (8+), student housing, senior housing, affordable, market-rate.

plain: The largest US real estate trade association — its members can call themselves Realtors and use the MLS.
snappy: Largest US real estate trade body; member Agents call themselves Realtors.
detail: NAR is the largest US trade association in any industry by membership — roughly 1.5 million member Agents. Member benefits include MLS access (often gated by NAR membership) and the right to use the trademarked title Realtor. The 2024 NAR settlement reshaped buy-side Commission economics: Buyer's Agent fees can no longer be posted on the MLS and must be negotiated directly with the buyer in a written agreement.

plain: Common shorthand for a Triple Net Lease — the commercial Lease where the Tenant pays Property Tax, insurance, and maintenance on top of base Rent.
snappy: Standard shorthand for a Triple Net Lease in Commercial Real Estate.
detail: NNN is universal industry shorthand for a Triple Net Lease. The three nets — Property Tax, insurance, common-area maintenance — sit on the Tenant. NNN deals trade on the strength of tenant credit and remaining Lease term; single-tenant NNN REITs (Realty Income, STORE Capital, W.P. Carey) built entire businesses around the structure. See Triple Net Lease for the full economics and how NNN compares to Gross Lease and Modified Gross Lease.

plain: An income property's gross rent minus its operating expenses — but before Mortgage payments and taxes on income.
snappy: Gross rental income minus operating expenses, before debt service.
detail: NOI is the income-side cornerstone of commercial real estate valuation. Equals gross potential rent, minus vacancy and credit loss, minus all operating expenses (Property Tax, insurance, utilities, repairs, management). It is reported before debt service (Mortgage Interest and Principal) and before federal income tax, so it isolates property performance from how the deal is financed or owned. NOI feeds Cap Rate, DSCR, and most institutional valuation models.

plain: A property use that was legal when established but no longer matches current Zoning — protected as 'grandfathered' from being shut down.
snappy: Pre-existing use that predates current Zoning and remains legal under a grandfather clause.
detail: When Zoning changes — a residential street rezoned office, a corner store district rezoned single-family — pre-existing uses get grandfathered as nonconforming. They can continue but face restrictions: most ordinances cap expansion, prohibit replacement after destruction, and treat abandonment (6-12 months of non-use, often) as termination. Property values for nonconforming uses are bounded by the right to keep doing the same thing — but new investment is risky. Variance or rezoning can convert nonconforming to conforming where political will allows.

plain: The flip side of Vacancy Rate — the percentage of units or square footage currently leased and paying Rent.
snappy: Percentage of units currently leased — the complement of Vacancy Rate.
detail: Occupancy is the headline operating metric most owners report. Physical occupancy counts units with signed Leases. Economic occupancy reflects actual Rent collected, accounting for concessions, bad debt, and below-market Leases. A property running 96% physical but 88% economic occupancy is hiding concession-driven vacancy. Stabilised commercial property typically targets 92-95% occupancy. Lease-up properties post lower occupancy as units fill; lenders set occupancy hurdles before releasing reserve funds or converting construction debt to permanent.

plain: A commercial building leased to businesses for white-collar work — single-tenant to high-rise, urban core to suburban park.
snappy: Commercial property leased to businesses for professional work.
detail: Office property covers Class A (newest, best-located, premium rents), Class B (older but well-maintained), Class C (older, deferred maintenance). Subtypes: urban core high-rise (CBD), suburban office park, medical office building (MOB), creative/flex office. Post-2020 remote-work shift hit Class B and Class C harder than Class A; sub-leasing surged. Lease terms typically run 5-10 years with Tenant Improvement allowances. NOI calculations use Effective Gross Income net of vacancy and concessions; underwriting weights tenant credit and remaining lease term heavily.

plain: The recurring costs of running an income property — Property Tax, insurance, utilities, repairs, management, but not Mortgage payments.
snappy: Recurring property costs subtracted from Gross Rental Income to compute NOI.
detail: Operating expenses split into fixed (Property Tax, insurance) and variable (utilities, repairs, management, payroll). They explicitly exclude debt service (Interest + Principal), capital expenditures (roof, HVAC replacement), depreciation, and income tax — those sit below the NOI line. Investors model operating expenses as a percentage of effective gross income; the 'OpEx ratio' typically runs 30–50% for stabilised Multifamily, 20–35% for industrial, higher for older properties or hospitality. Detailed line-item proformas are the bedrock of commercial underwriting.

plain: Anything you own that isn't Real Property — your furniture, your car, the curtains you can unscrew and take.
snappy: Movable property not permanently attached to Land — historically called chattel.
detail: Personal property is everything the homeowner can carry away without removing screws or breaking plaster. Free-standing appliances, furniture, art, drapes hung on rods that simply lift off. The line between personal property and a Fixture decides countless purchase-contract disputes — typical tests look at attachment method, intent, and whether removal causes damage. Mortgages don't usually cover personal property; secured loans on movables follow Article 9 of the UCC instead.

plain: A surveyor-drawn map showing how a subdivision is divided into Lots — the foundation document for every Lot's legal description.
snappy: Recorded subdivision map showing Lot boundaries, dimensions, and Easements.
detail: Plat maps get recorded at the county recorder's office when a developer subdivides raw Land. Each Lot is assigned a number; the legal description in subsequent Deeds references the plat ('Lot 12, Block 4, Sunny Acres Subdivision, recorded in Plat Book 87, Page 23'). Plats show streets, Easements, Setbacks, drainage, and any common areas. Re-platting (changing the Lot lines after recording) requires municipal approval and re-recording. A clean Plat is the foundation of clean Title for any subdivided property.

plain: Insurance you pay monthly on a Conventional Loan with less than 20% Down Payment — protects the Lender, not you.
snappy: Monthly insurance on conventional Mortgages with LTV above 80%.
detail: PMI applies to Conventional Loans with LTV above 80%. Costs 0.5-1.5% of loan amount annually depending on Credit Score and LTV, added to the monthly Mortgage payment. PMI automatically terminates when LTV reaches 78% based on the original Amortization schedule, or borrowers can request early cancellation at 80% if the property has appreciated and an Appraisal supports it. FHA Loans carry separate MIP that often runs for the loan's life.

plain: Upfront fees you can pay the Lender — discount points lower your rate; origination points pay the Lender's setup costs.
snappy: Upfront Mortgage fees; one point = 1% of loan amount.
detail: Points come in two types. Discount Points are prepaid interest that buys down the interest rate (typically 0.25% rate reduction per point, but the exact ratio varies). Origination points are the Lender's fee for processing the loan — pure cost, no rate benefit. Both show on the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure. The cost-vs-benefit math on Discount Points depends on how long the borrower keeps the Mortgage; break-even runs 5-7 years on typical loans.

plain: A Lender's written commitment, after running your finances, to lend you up to a specific amount.
snappy: Lender's documented commitment to fund a Mortgage up to a stated amount.
detail: Pre-approval requires submitting income documentation, credit pull, and asset verification — the Lender runs preliminary Underwriting and issues a letter committing to fund up to a specific loan amount subject to property review. Stronger than mere Pre-qualification (which relies on borrower-stated numbers). Pre-approval letters are typically valid 60-90 days and are now table-stakes in competitive offers.

plain: A quick estimate of how much you could borrow based on numbers you tell the Lender — no documents pulled.
snappy: Informal estimate of borrowing capacity based on stated, unverified information.
detail: Pre-qualification is the lightest form of Lender engagement — borrower states income, debts, and assets, the Lender runs a rough calculation, no credit pull. Useful as a first-pass budgeting tool. Many sellers no longer accept pre-qualification letters as proof of buying ability; Pre-approval is the credible signal. Some Lenders use the terms loosely or interchangeably — read the letter's fine print.

plain: The minimum annual return — usually 7-9% — that LPs must receive before the Sponsor earns any Promote.
snappy: Annual return rate paid to LPs before any Promote flows to the Sponsor.
detail: The Preferred Return (often 'pref') is the first economic tier after Return of Capital in a Waterfall. Common rates: 7-9% on Multifamily value-add deals, 6-8% on Core, higher on opportunistic. Cumulative vs non-cumulative matters — cumulative pref accrues unpaid amounts and compounds (LP friendly); non-cumulative resets each period (sponsor friendly). Some structures pay pref currently from cash flow; others defer to disposition. Pref does not guarantee LP returns — it just gates the Sponsor Promote.

plain: A fee some Mortgages charge if you pay off the loan early — banned on most residential loans since 2014.
snappy: Penalty charged for paying off a Mortgage ahead of schedule.
detail: Prepayment penalties protect Lenders against losing future Interest income when a borrower Refinances or sells early. After the 2008 crisis, Dodd-Frank and CFPB rules banned prepayment penalties on most residential Mortgages. They remain common on commercial Mortgages and on residential non-qualified Mortgages. Typical structures: a percentage of remaining Principal, a yield-maintenance calculation (commercial), or a defeasance arrangement (CMBS).

plain: The amount of money you actually borrowed, separate from the Interest you pay on it.
snappy: Outstanding Mortgage balance excluding accrued Interest.
detail: Each Mortgage payment splits between Interest (charged against current Principal) and Principal paydown (which reduces the balance). The Amortization schedule governs the split — early payments are mostly Interest, late ones mostly Principal. Extra payments toward Principal reduce total Interest cost and shorten the loan. Some Lenders apply extra payments to future installments instead of Principal unless explicitly instructed.

plain: A projected income statement for a property — Rent, vacancy, Operating Expenses, NOI — showing what the buyer expects the investment to produce.
snappy: Projected operating statement for a property over a defined hold period.
detail: Pro forma is the spreadsheet that underwrites any institutional commercial purchase. Top line: Gross Rental Income at market rents. Subtract vacancy, concessions, and bad debt → Effective Gross Income. Subtract Operating Expenses → NOI. Subtract debt service → cash flow to equity. Project annual growth (Rent escalations, expense inflation), Cap-Ex reserves, refinance assumptions, and Exit Cap Rate to model IRR. Aggressive pro formas with low Cap Rate exits and optimistic Rent growth are how deals lose money — sponsor track record at delivering against pro forma is what investors underwrite.

plain: The court process that handles a deceased owner's property — transfers it to heirs or buyers under will or state law.
snappy: Court process transferring a deceased owner's property to heirs.
detail: When an owner dies, real property either passes outside probate (joint Tenancy with right of survivorship, transfer-on-death deed, or property held in a living Trust) or through probate court. Probate authenticates the will (if any), pays creditors, settles taxes, and transfers Title to heirs. Probate sales are subject to court oversight and often slower than standard transactions. Probate property frequently trades at a discount because heirs prioritise speed and simplicity over price maximisation.

plain: The outsized share the Sponsor earns of profits earned by hitting return hurdles — typically 20-40% above the Preferred Return.
snappy: Outsized share the Sponsor earns of profits above the Preferred Return — Real Estate's carried interest.
detail: Promote aligns the Sponsor with LP outcomes. A typical structure: 0% Promote up to the Preferred Return (LP gets 100%), then 20-40% Promote above. Multi-tiered Promotes scale up as IRR exceeds higher hurdles — 20% Promote above 8% IRR, 30% above 12%, 40% above 18%. Promote crystallises at disposition or refinance, not annually. Tax-wise, Promote on holdings of 3+ years is taxed as long-term Capital Gain — the Real Estate equivalent of carried interest, politically scrutinised but largely intact through 2024.

plain: An annual tax on real estate paid to local government — usually a percentage of the property's Assessed Value.
snappy: Annual local tax on real property based on Assessed Value.
detail: Property Tax is the largest revenue source for US local governments — funding schools, police, fire, and infrastructure. The rate (the mill rate or millage) applies to the property's Assessed Value, not its market value. Typical effective rates range from 0.3% (Hawaii) to 2.5% (Illinois, New Jersey). Paid annually or semi-annually, often held in Escrow monthly with the Mortgage payment. Federal income tax allows a partial deduction subject to the SALT cap.

plain: Common shorthand for a Qualified Mortgage — the CFPB safe-harbour category for residential Mortgage origination.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Qualified Mortgage in residential Lending compliance.
detail: QM is the industry shorthand in residential Mortgage compliance for a Qualified Mortgage — the category of loans that meet the CFPB ability-to-repay safe harbour under Dodd-Frank. The acronym dominates conversation among Loan Officers, Underwriters, and compliance staff because the QM versus non-QM distinction drives loan pricing and litigation risk. See Qualified Mortgage for the substantive feature tests, DTI rules, and post-2020 price-based reform.

plain: A category of Mortgage created by the Dodd-Frank Act with conservative terms — capping DTI and banning risky features — that gives Lenders a legal safe harbour.
snappy: Mortgage meeting CFPB safe-harbour rules under Dodd-Frank — capped DTI, no risky features.
detail: Qualified Mortgage rules under the Dodd-Frank Act and CFPB's Regulation Z give Lenders protection from ability-to-repay lawsuits if they originate within the QM box. Original 2014 rules: DTI cap 43%, no interest-only, no negative amortisation, no balloon payment (except small Lenders), points and fees under 3% of loan. The 2020 'general QM' overhaul replaced the DTI cap with a price-based test. GSE-eligible loans automatically count as QM through the 'patch' (now expired post-2021 reforms). Non-QM lending exists but carries more litigation risk.

plain: A court action to clean up a confused Title — usually to resolve competing claims or remove old Liens.
snappy: Lawsuit to resolve competing Title claims and establish clear ownership.
detail: A quiet-title action is filed when ownership is uncertain — adverse possession claims, missing heirs in a Chain of Title, old Liens nobody can locate, boundary disputes, or fraud. The court resolves claims and issues a judgment confirming who holds Title. Once recorded, the judgment establishes clear Title that supports Title Insurance. Quiet-title actions can run 6-18 months and cost thousands; many sellers use them pre-listing to clear known clouds.

plain: A Deed that transfers whatever interest the grantor has — without any guarantee they actually own it.
snappy: Deed transferring interest without any warranty of Title.
detail: A Quitclaim Deed conveys whatever ownership interest the grantor has — which could be full Title, a partial interest, or nothing at all. No warranties of Title, no covenants, no protection for the grantee. Common in divorce property transfers (one spouse quitclaims to the other), family gifts, clearing minor Title defects, and adding/removing names from Title within a marriage. Almost never used in arm's length sales because the buyer has no Title recourse.

plain: A ceiling on how much an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage's interest rate can rise — per adjustment or over the loan's life.
snappy: Ceiling on ARM rate increases, per-period and lifetime.
detail: Rate Caps are the bedrock consumer protection in Adjustable-Rate Mortgages. Standard 5/1 ARMs carry 2/2/5 caps: 2% maximum first adjustment, 2% per subsequent adjustment, 5% lifetime. Without caps, a sudden Index spike could double a borrower's payment. The Lender must disclose caps on the Loan Estimate. Caps don't apply to the Margin — only to the rate itself after Index plus Margin is computed.

plain: Land plus everything permanently attached to it — buildings, fences, trees — distinct from movable personal property.
snappy: Land plus the buildings and improvements permanently attached to it.
detail: Real Estate is land and everything permanently affixed to it: buildings, in-ground pools, fences, perennial plantings, mineral rights, water rights, and Fixtures. Distinct from personal property (furniture, appliances not built in, vehicles), which moves with the owner. Synonymous with real property in most legal contexts. The bundle of rights — possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, and disposition — is what an owner actually buys when they take Title.

plain: The Land itself plus anything permanently attached — buildings, fences, the bedrock under your feet.
snappy: Land and everything permanently affixed to it — the legal opposite of Personal Property.
detail: Real property covers Land, structures, and Fixtures bolted into the land. It is the bundle of rights that gets conveyed by Deed, taxed via Property Tax, and recorded in the county registry. Movable items the seller takes when leaving (furniture, free-standing appliances) are Personal Property, not real property. Purchase contracts spell out which items count as Fixtures and travel with the sale.

plain: A real estate Agent who is a member of NAR and pledges to follow its Code of Ethics — not every Agent is a Realtor.
snappy: Real estate Agent who belongs to the National Association of Realtors.
detail: NAR has roughly 1.5 million members nationwide. Membership requires adherence to a 17-article Code of Ethics enforced through state-level boards. The trademark distinguishes Realtors from the broader pool of licensed Agents — but state licensure, not NAR membership, is what legally permits practice. The 2024 Burnett v. NAR settlement restructured commission practices: buyer Agents can no longer be paid through MLS-listed cooperative commissions; Buyer Representation Agreements with explicit fees are now standard.

plain: A loan where the Lender can chase the borrower's other assets — wages, savings, other property — if the collateral isn't enough to cover the debt after Foreclosure.
snappy: Loan where the lender can pursue the borrower personally if the collateral falls short.
detail: Most US residential Mortgages are non-recourse in some states (California, Arizona) and recourse in others (Texas, Florida) — the state's anti-deficiency statutes decide. Commercial Real Estate loans default to recourse unless explicitly structured as non-recourse with limited 'bad-boy' carve-outs (fraud, bankruptcy filing, environmental issues). Investors often pay 25–50 basis points more for non-recourse to wall off personal assets. Recourse status changes behaviour in distress: non-recourse borrowers walk away more readily; recourse borrowers fight harder.

plain: The historical (and illegal) practice of Lenders refusing Mortgages in mostly-minority neighbourhoods — drawn on actual red-line maps in the 1930s.
snappy: Race-based denial of Mortgage credit by neighbourhood — illegal but historically structural.
detail: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation produced colour-coded residential security maps in the 1930s, marking minority neighbourhoods in red as 'hazardous.' Banks used the maps to deny Mortgages and insurance for decades — the structural source of much of the 21st-century US racial wealth gap. Modern Redlining is illegal under the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, but persistence has been documented: CFPB and DOJ have brought multiple Redlining cases against banks in the 2020s for branch placement, marketing, and Underwriting practices.

plain: Replacing your current Mortgage with a new one — usually to lower the interest rate or pull out Equity.
snappy: Paying off an existing Mortgage with a new one, usually at a lower interest rate.
detail: Two main flavours: rate-and-term refinance (lower the rate or shorten the term, no cash out) and cash-out refinance (new larger loan, pocket the difference as cash). Both require fresh Closing Costs, Appraisal, and Underwriting. Break-even on a rate-and-term refi runs 2-4 years depending on Closing Costs and rate savings. Refinance activity is dominated by interest rate trends — the 2020-2021 rate trough triggered the largest refi wave in US history.

plain: An investor or developer's renovation of a property — somewhere between cosmetic touch-up and full gut renovation — done to lift value or Rent.
snappy: Renovation work intended to lift property value or rentable Rent.
detail: Rehab spans light cosmetic (paint, flooring, fixtures) to heavy structural (mechanical replacement, walls, layout changes, additions). Investor business plans frame Rehab as the value-creation engine in BRRRR and value-add Multifamily strategies: buy below-market, Rehab to lift the After-Repair Value (ARV), Refinance against the new value, recycle equity into the next deal. Hard Money frequently funds the buy-and-rehab phase; permanent debt takes out the rehab loan once the property is leased and stabilised.

plain: A public or private company that owns income-producing Real Estate — investors buy shares like a stock and receive a slice of the Rent.
snappy: Tax-advantaged entity that owns and operates income-producing property and distributes most earnings to shareholders.
detail: REITs pay no corporate income tax if they distribute at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders, hold at least 75% of assets in Real Estate, and earn at least 75% of income from rents or mortgage interest. Listed REITs trade on stock exchanges (Equinix, Simon, Prologis, AvalonBay). Non-traded and private REITs offer the same tax structure without daily liquidity. Subcategories: equity REITs (own buildings), mortgage REITs (own loans), hybrid. The structure dates to 1960, designed by Congress to democratise Real Estate Investment.

plain: The regular payment a Tenant makes to the Landlord in exchange for using the property.
snappy: Periodic payment from Tenant to Landlord under a Lease.
detail: Residential rent is usually paid monthly in advance. Commercial rent can be monthly or quarterly, often with annual escalations tied to CPI or fixed percentages. Late fees, NSF fees, and acceleration clauses appear in the Lease. Rent control laws cap residential rent increases in some cities (New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles) — usually with vacancy decontrol and tenant-protected categories. Commercial rent is typically quoted on a per-square-foot annual basis ($/SF/year) in the US.

plain: A property the Lender owns after a failed Foreclosure auction — now selling it to recover the loan.
snappy: Property owned by the Lender after Foreclosure auction failed to sell.
detail: REO inventory builds when Foreclosure auctions don't attract bidders above the Lender's reserve price — the property reverts to the Lender, who lists it for sale through an REO agent. Discount to market varies by Lender's hold tolerance and local market depth. REO sales typically use BPOs rather than full Appraisals for pricing decisions. Some investors specialise in REO acquisition for fix-and-flip or rental conversion.

plain: Money set aside each year — modeled in the pro forma — to fund predictable future Cap-Ex like roof, HVAC, and parking lot.
snappy: Annual reserve funded out of NOI to cover future Capital Expenditures.
detail: Lenders often require a Replacement Reserve to fund predictable Cap-Ex without depleting cash flow. Typical reserves: $250-$300 per unit per year for stabilised Multifamily, $0.20-$0.40 per square foot for Office and Retail. Reserves accumulate in a Lender-controlled account and draw down for approved Cap-Ex items. Underwriting models that skip the reserve overstate cash flow to equity by 1-3% of NOI — a common pro forma flag for sloppy underwriting. Reserves below NOI but above true cash flow is the standard placement.

plain: Real Estate intended primarily as a place for people to live — single-family homes, Condos, townhomes, and small Multifamily.
snappy: Real Estate held primarily for residential occupancy by owners or renters.
detail: Residential Real Estate covers properties intended as primary or secondary residences — Single-Family detached homes, Condos, townhomes, Co-ops, ADUs, and small Multifamily (1-4 units, which still qualify for residential Mortgage products like FHA Loans and VA Loans). 5+ unit Multifamily crosses into Commercial Real Estate for financing and Underwriting purposes. Residential transactions are far higher volume but lower individual size than commercial deals.

plain: A federal law regulating how settlement charges are disclosed and banning kickbacks between Lenders, title companies, and Agents.
snappy: Federal law governing settlement disclosures and prohibiting referral kickbacks.
detail: Enacted 1974. RESPA forces standardised settlement-cost disclosure (now folded into the TRID Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure since 2015), regulates Escrow accounts, and bans Section 8 kickbacks for referrals of settlement services. The line between marketing arrangements and illegal kickbacks remains the most litigated area — the CFPB has fined title companies, Lenders, and Agents tens of millions for violations. Borrowers also get a right to switch settlement providers and limits on Escrow over-collection.

plain: A commercial building leased to stores, restaurants, and services — strip centres, big boxes, malls, urban street retail.
snappy: Commercial property leased to consumer-facing stores, restaurants, and services.
detail: Retail subtypes: neighbourhood centre (grocery-anchored), community centre (junior anchor + smaller tenants), power centre (big-box tenants), regional and super-regional mall, lifestyle centre, outlet centre, urban street retail. E-commerce pressure has hit mall and Class B retail hardest; grocery-anchored neighbourhood centres have proven resilient. NNN Leases dominate single-tenant retail. Co-tenancy clauses (a tenant's right to break Lease if an anchor leaves) shape multi-tenant centre risk. Mixed-Use redevelopment of dead malls is a growing 2020s theme.

plain: What the property actually sold for — the number on the recorded Deed, not the original asking price.
snappy: Final agreed price at which a property changed hands.
detail: Sale Price is the dollar amount in the executed purchase contract, paid by the Buyer and received by the Seller (net of any concessions or credits). The Sale Price appears on the recorded Deed in most jurisdictions and is used to compute Property Tax transfer fees. List-to-Sale ratio compares Sale Price to the seller's original asking price — a market-temperature indicator (>100% = bidding war; <95% = soft market).

plain: The combined state and local taxes a homeowner pays — capped at $10,000 of federal deduction since the 2017 TCJA.
snappy: Combined state and local tax burden — federal deduction capped at $10,000 since TCJA.
detail: Before 2018, homeowners could deduct unlimited Property Tax plus state income tax against federal income. The TCJA capped the SALT deduction at $10,000 — a major hit to high-Property-Tax states (New York, New Jersey, California, Illinois, Massachusetts). High-income owners in those states lost five-to-six-figure deductions. Multiple states designed workaround entity-level pass-through taxes for business income (PTET), but residential homeowners have no equivalent escape. SALT-cap repeal has been a recurring political flashpoint; through 2024 the cap survived intact.

plain: The federal rent-subsidy program that helps low-income Tenants pay private-market Rent — vouchers cover the gap between income and Rent.
snappy: Federal rent subsidy paid to private Landlords on behalf of low-income Tenants.
detail: Section 8 (formally the Housing Choice Voucher Program, codified in Section 8 of the Housing Act of 1937 as amended) is the largest federal rental-assistance program — roughly 2.3 million households served. Tenants pay 30% of adjusted income; HUD pays the rest, up to a metro-area payment standard. Local public-housing authorities administer. Landlord acceptance is voluntary in most states; a growing list of states and cities bar Section-8 refusal as discrimination. Tenant turnover in Section-8 units is markedly lower than market — a feature that draws some private Landlords in.

plain: Money the Tenant pays upfront, held by the Landlord to cover damage or unpaid Rent at the end of the Lease.
snappy: Upfront deposit held by Landlord to secure Tenant performance under the Lease.
detail: State statutes cap residential security deposits at 1–2 months of Rent and require return (with itemised deductions) within 14–60 days of move-out. Some states require the deposit to sit in an interest-bearing escrow account, with interest paid to the Tenant. Wrongful withholding triggers statutory damages — often 2–3x the deposit plus attorney's fees. Commercial deposits face fewer statutory constraints; landlords often demand letters of credit or guarantees in addition to or instead of cash deposits.

plain: The party transferring ownership of a property — represented in the transaction by a Listing Agent.
snappy: Party transferring property in a real estate transaction.
detail: The Seller is the party transferring the property — an individual, a couple, an estate, an LLC, or a corporation. In most residential transactions the Seller works through a Listing Agent under a Listing Agreement. The Seller signs the Deed, pays the agreed Commission split from sale proceeds, and is bound by required Disclosure laws. Sellers may also offer concessions (credits at Closing) to sweeten an offer.

plain: The minimum required distance between a building and the property line — front, side, and rear — set by local Zoning.
snappy: Minimum distance between a building and the Lot line, set by Zoning.
detail: Setbacks shape the buildable envelope on every Lot. Single-family zones typically require 20-30 foot front, 5-15 foot side, 20-30 foot rear setbacks. Corner Lots have two front setbacks. Reduced setbacks are common in dense urban zones and for accessory structures. Building inside the setback creates an Encroachment requiring a Variance or removal. Setback violations are caught at Building Permit review or by a current Survey. Special setbacks apply to wetlands, slopes, easements, and historic districts.

plain: A line-by-line tally of every dollar at Closing — who pays what to whom — given to both Buyer and Seller.
snappy: Itemised list of all charges and credits at Closing for Buyer and Seller.
detail: Pre-TRID this was the HUD-1 statement, used for both residential and commercial. Since 2015, residential transactions use the Closing Disclosure; the ALTA Settlement Statement remains the standard for commercial deals and many investor purchases. The form shows Sale Price, Lender charges, title fees, recording fees, transfer taxes, Property Tax prorations, HOA prorations, and the final cash to close. Both sides sign at Closing. Discrepancies between Loan Estimate and final settlement statement above certain tolerances trigger TILA rescission rights.

plain: Selling a home for less than what's owed on the Mortgage, with the Lender agreeing to accept the shortfall instead of foreclosing.
snappy: Sale of property for less than the outstanding Mortgage with lender approval.
detail: A short sale is the polite alternative to Foreclosure. The owner negotiates with the Lender to accept a Sale Price below the loan balance and forgive the deficiency. Approval takes weeks to months — the lender wants proof of hardship, valuation evidence, and a buyer at market price. Forgiven debt is typically taxable as income, though the Mortgage Forgiveness Debt Relief Act provided periodic exemptions during the post-2008 crisis. Credit impact is significant but less severe than a completed Foreclosure.

plain: A detached home on its own Lot, designed for one household — the dominant US housing form.
snappy: Detached home on its own Lot, designed for a single household.
detail: Single-Family detached homes dominate the US housing stock, especially in suburbs. Each home sits on its own Lot, with no shared walls. Distinct from townhomes (attached but separately owned), Condos (units inside a larger building), and Multifamily (multiple rental units in one structure). Zoning that allows only single-family use is the most common American residential land-use designation — and the subject of recent reform debates in many cities.

plain: The replacement benchmark for LIBOR — what most Adjustable-Rate Mortgages now reset to.
snappy: Treasury-repo-based benchmark replacing LIBOR for ARM resets.
detail: SOFR is the Federal Reserve's chosen LIBOR successor — derived from actual overnight Treasury repo transactions rather than the survey-of-bank-quotes process that made LIBOR manipulable. The New York Fed publishes SOFR daily. Mortgages reference 30-day average SOFR (a backwards-looking compounded rate) plus Margin. SOFR is mechanically slightly different from LIBOR — typically lower, less volatile — so legacy LIBOR loans converted via a federally legislated spread adjustment.

plain: A one-time charge on property owners — by a city or an HOA — for specific improvements like a new sewer line, sidewalk, or roof replacement.
snappy: One-time charge for specific property improvements, levied by HOA or municipality.
detail: Municipal special assessments fund public improvements that benefit a defined district — sidewalks, sewer mains, sometimes lighting. They appear as a separate line on the Property Tax bill or as a private bond payment. HOA and Condo special assessments cover capital projects (roof, elevator, parking lot) that exceed the reserve fund. Buyers should ask for two years of HOA financials and minutes to see pending special assessments — an unfunded $30,000 roof can derail a deal. Disclosure is mandatory in most states.

plain: The active manager of a Real Estate syndication — finds the deal, raises equity, oversees operations, and earns a Promote for performance.
snappy: Active partner running a Real Estate syndication — origination, operations, and execution.
detail: The Sponsor is the GP in a typical Real Estate LP structure. Brings the deal, leads due diligence, executes the business plan, manages day-to-day operations, communicates with Limited Partners. Earns three layers of compensation: acquisition fee (1-2% of purchase price), asset-management fee (1-2% of equity per year), and a Promote (share of profits above an IRR hurdle). LPs underwrite the Sponsor track record, alignment of interests, and reporting discipline as carefully as the deal itself. Bad Sponsors lose investor capital regardless of market.

plain: A property that has reached its target Occupancy Rate and steady-state Operating Expenses — the point where Cap Rates and NOI become meaningful.
snappy: Property at target Occupancy Rate and normalised Operating Expenses — fit for Cap Rate analysis.
detail: Stabilisation matters for both underwriting and lending. A newly developed Multifamily property typically takes 12-24 months to stabilise; commercial Office can take longer. Pre-stabilisation, NOI is depressed by Lease-up vacancy and ramping operating costs — so Cap Rate analysis distorts. Construction Loans usually convert to permanent financing only after a stabilisation hurdle (debt-service coverage, occupancy threshold). Acquisition underwriting often projects 'going-in' NOI off Stabilized assumptions, even if current operations haven't reached them.

plain: An illegal Real Estate Agent practice of guiding Buyers toward or away from neighbourhoods based on protected characteristics — race, family status, religion.
snappy: Illegal Agent practice of channeling Buyers toward or away from areas by protected class.
detail: Steering violates the Fair Housing Act. Examples: telling a Black Buyer that 'they'd be more comfortable' in one neighbourhood, declining to show listings outside a stereotyped 'family' or 'retiree' area, characterising school quality by demographic proxy. Steering can be subtle and is hard to prove — NAR ethics training emphasises identical service regardless of perceived characteristics. Newsday's 2019 fair-housing investigation in Long Island and subsequent enforcement actions revived public attention. Brokerages train and audit to manage liability.

plain: A tax rule that resets a property's cost basis to its market value at the owner's death — heirs sell with little or no Capital Gain.
snappy: Reset of property's tax basis to fair market value at the owner's death.
detail: Step-up in basis is one of the largest tax breaks in US Real Estate. Heirs inherit at fair market value at date of death; if they sell shortly after, Capital Gain is minimal. A property bought for $200,000 forty years ago and worth $1.2M at owner's death gets stepped up to $1.2M basis — the heir avoids tax on $1M of appreciation. Community Property states grant a full step-up on both halves at the death of one spouse; common-law states grant only half-step-up. Political pressure to limit or eliminate step-up has not (through 2024) produced major reform.

plain: When a Tenant rents the property out to someone else for part or all of the remaining Lease term.
snappy: Tenant's rental of the leased premises to a third party for some or all of the term.
detail: The Tenant remains liable to the Landlord under the original Lease, while the subtenant pays the original Tenant. Most leases require Landlord consent for sublease, sometimes with reasonable-consent standards (especially commercial) or absolute discretion (typical residential). Assignment, by contrast, transfers the whole Lease — original Tenant exits entirely. Commercial sublease is common when companies downsize but face long remaining terms; rent gap (sublease rent below contract rent) is the original Tenant's loss to bear.

plain: A professional measurement of property boundaries, structures, and Easements — produces a drawing used at Closing and for new construction.
snappy: Boundary and improvement measurement of a property by a licensed surveyor.
detail: Surveys come in flavours of precision. A boundary survey marks the property lines (corner monuments, dimensions). An ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey is the institutional standard for commercial transactions — boundary plus structures, Easements, encroachments, flood zone, and improvements. A mortgage location survey is cheaper, used for residential refi. Lenders often require a current survey at Closing. Surveys surface Encroachments, missing setbacks, and unrecorded Easements that Title Insurance might otherwise miss.

plain: The 2017 federal tax law that cut corporate rates, capped the state and local tax deduction, and reshaped Real Estate tax treatment.
snappy: 2017 federal tax overhaul affecting depreciation, 1031 Exchange scope, and the SALT deduction.
detail: TCJA's Real Estate impacts run wide. Mortgage interest deduction was capped at $750,000 of acquisition debt (down from $1M); HELOC interest only deductible for substantial improvements. State and Local Tax (SALT) deduction capped at $10,000 — devastating in high-Property-Tax states. Section 199A pass-through deduction extended to qualified Real Estate businesses. Bonus Depreciation expanded to 100% then phasing down to zero by 2027. 1031 Exchange restricted to Real Property only; personal-property exchanges eliminated.

plain: The right and condition of holding property as a Tenant under a Lease — also the collective term for the various co-ownership forms (Joint Tenancy, Tenancy in Common, Tenancy by the Entirety).
snappy: Right or condition of holding property as Tenant — also the collective term for co-ownership forms.
detail: Two distinct senses share the word. (1) Leasehold tenancy: the Tenant's possessory right under a Lease — periodic (month-to-month), term (fixed Lease), sufferance (Holdover Tenant), at will. (2) Co-ownership tenancy: the umbrella for Joint Tenancy, Tenancy in Common, and Tenancy by the Entirety — the various forms of multi-owner Title. Context disambiguates. The shared root makes sense — both senses describe the right of holding, just from different angles (occupying versus owning).

plain: A form of joint ownership available only to married couples — strongest creditor protection of any co-ownership form.
snappy: Marital co-ownership form with right of survivorship and joint-creditor protection.
detail: Recognised in roughly half the states (Florida, New York, Ohio, Massachusetts among them). Tenancy by the Entirety requires marriage and treats the spouses as a single legal entity owning the property. A creditor of just one spouse cannot reach the property — creditors of both can. Right of survivorship at death is automatic. Divorce typically converts Tenancy by the Entirety to Tenancy in Common. The structure is favoured for primary-residence asset protection where state law allows.

plain: Two or more owners hold the property together — but each share passes to the owner's heirs at death, not to the co-owners.
snappy: Co-ownership where each share is independently inheritable and transferable.
detail: Tenancy in common is the default form when a Deed conveys to multiple buyers without specifying Joint Tenancy. Shares can be unequal (60/40, 70/30) and each owner can sell or will their interest independently. Common in investment partnerships and unmarried co-buyers. No survivorship — a deceased owner's share goes through Probate to heirs, who become new co-tenants. Co-tenants share rights to possess the whole property, regardless of percentage ownership.

plain: The person or business renting a property under a Lease — pays Rent, follows the rules, has the right to possess the space.
snappy: Person or entity occupying leased property in exchange for Rent.
detail: Tenants get rights that pre-empt many private contract terms. The right to a habitable dwelling, quiet enjoyment, security-deposit protection, and proper Eviction procedure all flow from state and (in some cities) local statute. Commercial tenants have weaker statutory rights — they negotiate protections into the Lease. Subleases let a tenant transfer occupancy to a third party, usually with Landlord consent. Holdover tenants who stay past lease expiration become month-to-month or trigger Eviction depending on Landlord response.

plain: Money the Landlord spends — or credits the Tenant for — to customise a leased space before the Tenant moves in.
snappy: Landlord allowance or work funding interior customisation of leased space for a Tenant.
detail: TI dollars are heavily negotiated in Commercial Lease economics. The Landlord typically offers a per-square-foot allowance ($25-$150 PSF depending on market and Lease length) to fund Tenant-specific Build-Out — partitions, finishes, mechanical changes, IT cabling. The TI investment is amortised into the base Rent or treated as Lease-level Capital Expenditure by the Landlord. Long Leases justify higher TI; short Leases get little or none. Unused TI typically reverts to the Landlord.

plain: A federal law making Lenders disclose the full cost of credit in standard form — APR, finance charges, payment schedule.
snappy: Federal disclosure law standardising how Lenders quote the cost of credit.
detail: Enacted 1968, now living inside Regulation Z. TILA forces lenders to disclose APR, total finance charges, payment schedule, and right of rescission on standardised forms. Residential Mortgage disclosures fold into the TRID combined disclosure (Loan Estimate + Closing Disclosure) since 2015. Violations carry private rights of action: rescission within three years on refinances, statutory damages on disclosure errors. The CFPB administers and enforces TILA against bank and non-bank lenders.

plain: Legal ownership of a property — proven by a Deed and protected by Title Insurance.
snappy: Legal ownership of real property, evidenced by a Deed.
detail: Title is the bundle of legal rights to a property. A Deed transfers Title from grantor to grantee. Title can be encumbered by Liens, easements, or other claims — Title Insurance protects against undiscovered defects. Title is held in various forms: fee simple (full ownership), joint tenancy (with right of survivorship), tenancy in common (separately transferable shares), or tenancy by the entirety (married couples).

plain: A neutral third party that researches Title, issues Title Insurance, and handles the Escrow at Closing in most states.
snappy: Neutral third party that researches Title, insures it, and runs the Escrow at Closing.
detail: Title companies sit at the centre of US residential Closings. The title search examines public records for Deeds, Liens, judgments, Easements, and Encroachments. The Title Insurance commitment outlines what the insurer will and won't cover. The escrow officer collects funds from Buyer and Lender, pays off prior loans, records the new Deed, and disburses the seller's proceeds. In attorney states (New York, Massachusetts, much of the Northeast), attorneys play this role instead. Compensation comes from title premiums and escrow fees.

plain: Insurance protecting the buyer (and Lender) against undiscovered defects in the property's Title.
snappy: One-time insurance against Title defects undiscovered at Closing.
detail: Title Insurance differs from other insurance — it covers past events (missed Liens, fraud, recording errors), not future ones, and is paid once at Closing. Two policies: the owner's policy protects the buyer; the lender's policy (mandatory if there's a Mortgage) protects the Lender for the loan amount. Title Insurance follows a search of public records by the title company; defects found before Closing become buyer's negotiation leverage.

plain: The historical review of public records that confirms who owns a property and what Liens or Easements attach to it.
snappy: Examination of public records to confirm ownership and surface Encumbrances.
detail: The title search is the engine behind Title Insurance. A title abstractor or attorney pulls every recorded document affecting the property — Deeds, mortgages, judgment Liens, mechanic's Liens, tax Liens, Easements, court judgments — back to the original Land grant or a statutory cut-off. Gaps in the Chain of Title, unreleased Liens from prior owners, and forgeries are common issues to surface. The title commitment lists exceptions the insurer won't cover; clean Closings require curing those before funding.

plain: Bonds issued by the US federal government — the 10-year Treasury yield is the main benchmark for fixed Mortgage rates.
snappy: US government bond; the 10-year yield benchmarks Mortgage rates.
